endorsements.quote: The real promise lies in a “clinician-in-the-loop” approach: AI may perform a first pass at gathering relevant evidence and organizing raw material, but human experts must interpret the findings and decide which leads warrant further exploration.
Provenance: Can each key claim be traced to a peer-reviewed source? Routinely spot-check citations against full texts.

Journals and funding bodies should demand complete transparency whenever manuscripts lean on AI, whether it helped mine the literature or draft prose, and hold authors accountable for any undisclosed reliance.
A pragmatic norm would be to disclose AI involvement in plain language and to confirm understanding with a brief teach-back.

unlisted_practices: Medical educators should incorporate critical appraisal of AI outputs into their curricula.
Peer reviewers should demand clear source citations and verify dubious claims.
Health system leadership should vet a toolkit of in-depth research services and establish protocols for monitoring AI-generated evidence.
Health systems and training programs should allocate resources for equitable access to vetted AI tools.
Health systems and training programs should offer faculty development in AI literacy.
Health systems and training programs should audit AI use for disparate impact.
Clinicians should weight evidence from AI-assisted synthesis by privileging randomized trials and high-quality meta-analyses.
Clinicians should request counter-summaries from AI tools and compare claims with sources to check for bias.
Clinicians should disclose AI-shaped syntheses to colleagues or patients and retain human responsibility for conclusions.

screen.reason: This is a viewpoint/framework paper proposing clinician-in-the-loop duties and institutional policies/guardrails for using LLMs and deep research systems in evidence synthesis.
